But what exactly does "value-added" mean here? Think of consumer data not just as a record of past purchases, but as a powerful lens through which suppliers can anticipate future behavior. Every click, every scroll, every time a shopper hovers over a product image—these actions form a digital footprint that, when analyzed, reveals patterns in what people like, how they compare options, and when they're likely to buy.
In recent years, information technology companies and e-commerce platforms have developed

systems for shopping, based on customer feedback and customer behavior predictions, to build virtual platforms for real-time communication or human–computer response between suppliers and customers in online shopping environments (Cho et al., 2006; Rajamma et al., 2009).

Imagine a digital marketplace that doesn’t just display products, but actively listens and responds—like a knowledgeable salesperson who remembers your preferences, notices when you’re hesitating, and offers just the right suggestion at the right time. That’s the goal of these intelligent systems: to simulate a personalized, responsive shopping experience, even in a fully online setting.

The primary aim of this is to reduce customers' search costs and evaluation errors when they are faced with similar kinds of product information (Brynjolfsson et al., 2011; Nagar and Gandotra, 2016), which is key to providing customers with optimal consumption choice.

Let’s unpack that. “Search costs” aren’t just about money—they include the time, effort, and mental energy you spend comparing dozens of nearly identical blenders or headphones. When products look alike and descriptions are vague, it’s easy to make a poor choice or give up altogether. This is where smart systems step in. By learning from millions of past interactions, they can filter out irrelevant options and highlight the ones that best match your needs, dramatically cutting down confusion and decision fatigue.
Big data analytics (BDA) and machine learning (ML) can be used to change the traditional supply chain design and product operation mode (Li et al., 2015).

Traditionally, supply chains were built around forecasting demand using historical sales data—essentially, looking in the rearview mirror. But BDA and ML allow companies to look forward, predicting what customers will want before they even know it themselves. It’s like upgrading from a static map to a live GPS that adjusts in real time based on traffic, weather, and your driving habits.

Suppliers can provide personalized and customized services based on data analysis results, finding potential customer demand from the perspective of the demand chain (Li et al., 2018), and then apply them to the whole process of supply chain management (SCM).

The “demand chain” flips the traditional model: instead of pushing products based on what’s easy to make or stock, companies pull insights directly from customer behavior to shape everything from inventory to delivery.

For example, suppliers can use click data to understand consumer psychology and the behavior of visiting users (potential shoppers) and then customize complementary products of recommended packages and promotional activities for these visiting users (Carmona et al., 2012; Ding et al., 2015; Mishra et al., 2018), thus improving service quality and consumers' experience of suppliers (Cohen, 2018).

Think of how Amazon suggests “frequently bought together” items—those aren’t random. They’re the result of algorithms detecting subtle patterns in millions of shopping carts, revealing what items tend to go together, like peanut butter and jelly, or a phone and a case.

These “accurate forecasts” can promote the explosive growth of regional economies, especially in relation to special events or festivals. For example, the “Double 11” (11 November) 10th Shopping Festival in China in 2018 generated a trading volume exceeding 300bn yuan on that day, and the total trading volume in 15 h on that day exceeded the total trading in any 24 h for 2017.

That’s not just a sales spike—it’s a logistical earthquake. To handle such volume, supply chains must be not only fast but predictive. Warehouses need to pre-position goods based on anticipated demand, delivery fleets must be scaled in advance, and customer service systems must be ready for a surge in inquiries. All of this hinges on the ability to forecast with high precision, and that’s where data-driven models become indispensable.

The online shopping market has seen unprecedented prosperity. However, with the development of online shopping, data sources and structures are becoming increasingly complex, and the sustainable development of SCM is also facing new challenges (Panigrahi et al., 2019; Song et al., 2019a, b). The phenomenon of online suppliers finding it hard to retain customers is also becoming increasingly obvious (He et al., 2019; Liao et al., 2017; Swaid and Wigand, 2009).

Here’s a paradox: even though we have more data than ever, keeping customers loyal is harder than ever. Why? Because choice is abundant, switching is effortless, and attention is scarce. A customer can abandon a cart with one click and land on a competitor’s site in seconds.

Many studies have used “customer lifetime value” (CLV) to describe the relationship between consumers and suppliers, and “customer loyalty” and “repurchasing” are important indicators in measuring consumers’ purchase behavior (Blattberg et al., 2009).

CLV is a powerful concept—it shifts the focus from a single transaction to the entire relationship. Instead of asking, “How much did this customer spend today?” companies ask, “How much will this customer spend over the next five years?” This long-term view changes everything: it justifies investing in better service, personalized offers, and loyalty programs, because the payoff comes over time.

In fact, the actual “lifetime” of consumers is an important reason for CLV. Online searching and the comparison of product information are shopping strategies that most of us adopt (Hamouda, 2019; Price Waterhouse Coopers, 2015; Verhoef et al., 2015). When we look online for goods on retail websites, it does not necessarily lead to direct purchases. About 80% of the time, we will choose not to purchase goods placed in the shopping cart (Kukar-Kinney and Scheinbaum, 2009).

This is known as cart abandonment, and it’s one of the biggest puzzles in e-commerce. But here’s the key insight: just because someone doesn’t buy *now* doesn’t mean they’re not valuable. Their browsing history, time spent on pages, and items added to cart all signal interest. It’s like someone test-driving a car—they might not buy it that day, but they’re clearly in the market.
Moreover, the fierce competition among merchants is also an important reason for the low loyalty of consumers.

With dozens of websites offering similar products, often at comparable prices, the deciding factor becomes experience: how easy is it to find what you want? How fast is delivery? How helpful is customer service? But even more subtly, it’s about feeling understood. A shopper who receives relevant recommendations feels seen; one who gets irrelevant ads feels ignored.

However, in some research on the purchase behavior of online consumers, it has found that, even if users search and visit shopping websites, they may not purchase goods, but that their browsing history and behavior information are still valuable, as they can help explain customers’ behavioral intention, which is crucial for online sellers to accurately recommend goods (Plummer, 1974).

Behavioral intention is a psychological precursor to action—it’s the “I might buy this” stage. By analyzing digital footprints, companies can detect this intention and intervene with timely offers, reminders, or incentives to convert interest into action.

In order to solve the aforementioned problems, attempts have been made to improve pricing strategies by predicting customers' purchase intention behavior, so as to improve the purchase rate of customers (Budnikas, 2015; Fernandes and Teixeira, 2015).

For instance, dynamic pricing—adjusting prices in real time based on demand, competition, and user behavior—can be fine-tuned if you know how likely a customer is to buy. A hesitant shopper might receive a limited-time discount; a loyal one might get free shipping. These are not random promotions—they’re strategic nudges based on predictive models.

Based on these discussions, this paper will build two empirical models, from the supply side and the demand side, of the online service supply chain (OSSC). The first model uses an ML algorithm to analyze, from the big data samples on the demand side, the important factors that affect the purchase behavior of customers.

This means digging into real-world data—clicks, time on page, cart additions, past purchases—to identify which signals most strongly predict an actual purchase. Is it how many times someone views a product? Whether they read reviews? The time of day they shop? The model will learn which features matter most.

That’s exactly the idea behind a **Stackelberg game**—a strategic interaction in game theory where one player, the *leader*, makes a decision first (like setting a price or output level), and the other player, the *follower*, observes that decision and then chooses their own best response. It's like a chess match where one player moves first, and the second player adjusts their strategy accordingly.

In our context, the **service integrator**—think of them as the orchestrator of the entire service offering, perhaps a platform like Amazon or Alibaba that bundles various services—acts as the leader. They decide on a pricing strategy first. The **service provider**—say, a third-party seller or a logistics partner—then reacts by setting their own price or service level in a way that maximizes their own benefit, given the integrator’s move.

This setup is especially realistic in online service supply chains (OSSCs), where platforms have more market power and visibility than individual providers. By modeling this interaction as a Stackelberg game, we can uncover the *optimal pricing strategies* for both parties: not just what prices they *should* set, but how their decisions influence each other.

Now we shift perspective—from the supply side to the customer. What makes someone click “buy”?

Customers don’t make decisions in a vacuum. Their choices are shaped by many factors: price, reviews, delivery speed, brand trust, website design, even how easy it is to return an item. But which of these matters *most*?

This question digs into **demand-side behavior**—the psychology and habits of online shoppers. By analyzing real customer data (perhaps using the feature selection from RQ1), we aim to pinpoint the *key driver* of purchase intention. Is it price? Convenience? Social proof? Once we know, we can focus our strategies on what truly moves the needle.

**RQ3.
From the supply-side analysis, how does the most important factor for customer purchase intention (obtained from the demand-side analysis) affect the supply-side optimal pricing strategy in

OSSCs?**  
Here’s where everything comes together. Suppose RQ2 reveals that *delivery speed* is the biggest factor in whether customers buy. Great—but what should the service integrator and provider *do* about it?

This third question bridges the gap between customer behavior and business strategy. If customers care deeply about fast delivery, then the supply chain must adapt. Maybe the integrator needs to incentivize faster shipping, or the provider must invest in logistics. But these improvements cost money—so how should prices be adjusted to stay profitable?

By feeding the insights from demand (RQ2) into the Stackelberg game model, we can simulate how the leader and follower should set prices when a key customer preference changes. This turns customer insights into actionable, profit-maximizing strategies.

In short, this study follows a clear, logical arc:  
1. Use smart ML tools to handle big data efficiently (RQ1),  
2. Discover what customers truly care about (RQ2),  
3. Use that knowledge to optimize pricing in a realistic leader-follower market (RQ3).

### 4.1 Analysis of the influencing factors of customer behavior intention

Our goal here is to answer a critical business question: *What aspects of a customer’s online experience most strongly predict whether they will make a purchase?* To answer this, we analyze large-scale, real-world data on how customers interact with e-commerce websites. But raw data contains many variables—some useful, some not. So our strategy is twofold:

1. **Identify the most important features** (i.e., variables) that influence customer behavior using a process called *feature selection*. This helps us focus only on what truly matters.
2. **Compare different machine learning models** to see which one best predicts customer behavior—both before and after removing less important features. This tells us not only *what* drives behavior but also *how reliably* we can predict it.

We test four popular classification models:
- **Decision Tree (DT)**: A model that splits data using a tree-like structure based on feature values.
- **Logistic Regression (LR)**: A statistical model that estimates the probability of a binary outcome (like purchase vs. no purchase).
- **Support Vector Machine (SVM)**: A model that finds the best boundary between different classes (e.g., buyers vs. non-buyers).
- **Random Forest (RF)**: An ensemble method that combines many decision trees to improve accuracy and reduce overfitting.

To ensure our results are robust and not just due to chance, we use **fivefold cross-validation** (Han et al., 2019). Here’s how it works:  
Imagine you have 100 data points. You divide them into 5 equal groups (folds) of 20. You train your model on 4 folds (80 data points) and test it on the remaining 1 fold (20 data points). You repeat this process 5 times, each time using a different fold for testing. Then, you average the results across all 5 runs. This gives a more reliable estimate of how well your model will perform on new, unseen data.

We measure performance using the **average ROC value** (Receiver Operating Characteristic), which tells us how well a model distinguishes between classes (e.g., buyers vs. non-buyers). A higher ROC value (closer to 1.0) means better predictive performance.

Here’s what we found:

**(1) Decision Tree (DT):**  
- Without feature selection: average ROC = 0.7333  
- With feature selection: average ROC = 0.7349 (see Figure 1)  
→ A very slight improvement. DT doesn’t benefit much from removing features, possibly because it already ignores less important ones during splitting.

**(2) Logistic Regression (LR):**  
- Without feature selection: average ROC = 0.8965  
- With feature selection: average ROC = 0.8970 (see Figure 2)  
→ A small but consistent gain. LR benefits from cleaner data, as irrelevant features can distort its probability estimates.

**(3) Support Vector Machine (SVM):**  
- Without feature selection: average ROC = 0.7914  
- With feature selection: average ROC = 0.8011 (see Figure 3)  
→ A modest improvement. SVM is sensitive to noise, so removing irrelevant features helps it find a better decision boundary.

**(4) Random Forest (RF):**  
- Without feature selection: average ROC = 0.8853  
- With feature selection: average ROC = 0.8853 (see Figure 4)  
→ No change in performance. Why? Because RF already performs *built-in feature selection* during training—it naturally focuses on the most important variables and downweights or ignores the rest. So pre-filtering doesn’t add extra value for RF.

> **Why does this matter?**  
Even though RF’s accuracy didn’t improve, feature selection still has practical benefits: it removes redundant or irrelevant data, making it faster and easier for suppliers to interpret customer behavior. In real business settings, time and clarity are crucial. A smaller, cleaner dataset allows decision-makers to act quickly without getting lost in noise.

Now, let’s look at *which* features actually matter most.

From Figure 5, which ranks the importance of 17 different factors in predicting customer behavior, one variable stands out dramatically: **page value**.

> **What is page value?**  
Think of it as a measure of how valuable a webpage is to a customer in terms of driving a purchase. Technically, it’s calculated as the average value a page contributes to a transaction. For example, if a product page is often viewed right before a purchase, it gets a high page value. It reflects both the *relevance* and *conversion potential* of a page.

The results show that **page value has an importance score greater than 0.5**, far surpassing the next most important features. To put this in perspective, the total importance across all 17 features sums to 1.0, so a single feature scoring over 0.5 dominates the model’s decision-making.

Other notable factors include:
- **Exit rate**: How often users leave the site from a given page.
- **Product-related duration**: Time spent on product-related pages.
- **Bounce rate**: Percentage of visitors who leave after viewing only one page.
- **Related products**: How many associated items are viewed.
- **Month**: Seasonal trends in behavior.

These insights are powerful for retailers. For instance, a high bounce rate on a product page might signal poor design or misleading content. A high page value suggests that the page is effective at guiding users toward a purchase.

In short, **page value isn’t just a metric—it’s a proxy for information quality and service clarity**. When customers can easily find and understand product details, they’re more likely to buy. This has direct implications for how services should be presented online.

### 4.2 Analysis of optimal pricing strategy

Now that we’ve identified the key driver of customer behavior—**page value**—we shift to the supply side. The question becomes: *How should suppliers set prices when they know that better information (reflected in higher page values) leads to more purchases?*

From the demand-side analysis, we see that **page value strongly influences purchase decisions**. But what does this mean in practical business terms? It suggests that the way a service is *presented*—its clarity, detail, and navigability—directly affects customer demand. In other words, **page value acts as a measure of service visualization**: how well the service is communicated and understood online.

When customers view more pages related to a product (and those pages have high page values), they gain a clearer picture of what they’re buying. This reduces uncertainty—what economists call *information opacity*—and increases the likelihood of purchase. So, the **average number of pages viewed** and their **associated page values** are not just behavioral metrics; they are indicators of service quality and customer confidence.

Given this, we propose a strategic response: **incorporate page value into the pricing model of the online service supply chain (OSSC)**. But how?

Large firms with market power—such as e-commerce platforms or tech companies—often act as intermediaries. They don’t produce the service themselves but connect customers with service providers. These firms can:

**Step 1: Analyze the follower’s (SP’s) decision.**

Suppose the SI has already chosen a price $ p $. Now the SP wants to pick $ e $ to maximize its profit in equation (4). Since $ p $ is already fixed (from the SP’s perspective), we treat it as a constant when optimizing over $ e $.

Set this equal to zero for optimality:

Now let’s tackle RQ2: *Which factors most strongly influence a customer’s decision to buy?* The researchers analyzed 17 total features—variables that could potentially affect shopping behavior—and ranked them by importance.

And the winner is: **page value**.

But what *is* page value? Let’s make this concrete. Imagine you’re browsing an online store. You click on a product—say, a pair of wireless headphones. The page loads with high-resolution images, a detailed description, customer reviews, videos showing the product in use, comparison charts, and maybe even a live chat option. That page isn’t just informative—it’s valuable. **Page value** quantifies how much *potential revenue* a page contributes to the site, based on how users interact with it and how likely they are to convert (i.e., make a purchase) after viewing it.

But here’s the deeper insight: **page value acts as a proxy for information quality**. The richer and more visually engaging the content, the higher the page value—and the more trust and interest it generates in the customer. Think of it like a digital salesperson: the better it communicates, the more persuasive it becomes.

So when the study says page value has the *most significant impact*, it’s really saying: **clear, rich, well-structured product information drives purchases**. It’s not enough to just list a product’s name and price—modern shoppers demand context, clarity, and confidence.

Now, what about the other important features?

- **Product-related duration**: How long a user spends on product-related pages. Longer time usually means higher interest.
- **Related products**: How many similar or complementary items the user views. This reflects exploration and consideration.
- **Exit rate**: The likelihood a user leaves the site after viewing a page. A high exit rate on a product page might signal poor information quality or mismatched expectations.

These are all **numerical features**—they’re measured in numbers, so they’re easy to plug into models. But here’s a surprise: even **month**, a **categorical feature**, carries substantial weight.

Wait—why would the *month* matter?

Because shopping behavior changes with seasons, holidays, promotions, and cultural events. For example, December likely sees spikes in electronics and gift purchases, while back-to-school months boost sales of laptops and stationery. So even though “month” isn’t about the product itself, it captures **temporal patterns in consumer demand**—a powerful signal in predictive modeling.
